newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts divided about possible new Riksbank goal.
newsitem.headline: Analysts divided about possible new Riksbank goal.

text.p: Swedish politicians are reported to be discussing giving the central bank a secondary unemployment target on top of its current sole price stability aim, but analysts have mixed views on such a move.

Some analysts do not see a secondary target damaging the Riksbank's credibility, while others fear an unemployment target will put the central bank under pressure to loosen monetary policies when the inflation target is not threatened.
Currently, the Riksbank's only target is price stability, to keep inflation at two percent with an allowed deviation of one percentage point on either side.

Daily Dagens Industri reported on Wednesday that the minority Social Democratic government and its informal cooperation partner, the Centre Party, wanted to set secondary central bank targets for unemployment and growth.
But Finance Minister Erik Asbrink dismissed the article.
"It is founded on rumours that are completely misleading and false...the rumours come from ignorance about how the situation is in other countries," Asbrink told a news conference.
"Almost all central banks in EU (the European Union) and outside the EU have a price stability target and one secondary target to support economic policies, employment and so on," Asbrink said.
Anders Hahnel, chief economist at Aragon brokerage, was not too worried about a possible secondary target.
"What's going on is rather an adjustment to ECB (the European central bank)," he told Reuters.

"I think the Riksbank will remain just as credible as today, on the condition you don't put the unemployment target on par with the price stability target. That would have a very negative effect on interest rates."
Analyst Anders Olshov at Nordbanken and economist Knut Hallberg at Swedbank agreed.
"If they express themselves clearly so there is no doubt about the price stability target being the principal goal, we don't have much to say about a secondary target," Olshov said.
But Hallberg said the timing could be bad as there was still uncertainty about Sweden's view on membership in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).
Prime Minister Goran Persson said on Wednesday the government would announce its opinion on EMU by the end of May.
Other economists also worried about a change.

"The Riksbank's position does not enjoy full credibility," Carl B Hamilton, chief economist at Handelsbanken, said. "In England they moved toward an independant central bank with an inflation target. This would go in the opposite direction."
Hamilton added that a secondary target would put pressure on the bank to loosen monetary policy when the inflation target was not threatened.
"I want to stress that there is a big difference in having an old instruction with several targets and introducing new secondary targets," Hamilton said.
Other economists agreed.
"I don't think it's a good signal," Peter Lindqvist, analyst HSBC Midland, said.

"You can always say that other central banks also have several targets but market players have more confidence in them," he said, adding that he did not expect the European central bank to have dual targets.
